claim: Expression of Sgs3-GFP begins at 96–100 h AEL.
source: Expression of Sgs3-GFP begins at 96–100 h AEL, and can be detected at the distal region of the gland (Figure 1C).

evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sgs3-GFP expression expands to more proximal cells over time.
source: Later on, Sgs3-GFP expression expands to more proximal cells, and at 116 h AEL, the mucin becomes detectable in the whole gland, with the exception of ductal cells which do not express Sgs3 (Figure 1C; Biyasheva et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C, supported by citation.

evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C, supported by citation.

claim: At 116–120 h AEL, SGs fuse with the apical plasma membrane in response to an ecdysone peak.
source: Thereafter, at 116–120 h AEL, in response to an ecdysone peak, SGs fuse with the apical plasma membrane, and release their content to the gland lumen (Figure 1C).

claim: SGs release their content to the gland lumen at 116–120 h AEL.
source: Thereafter, at 116–120 h AEL, in response to an ecdysone peak, SGs fuse with the apical plasma membrane, and release their content to the gland lumen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SGs enlarge from 96 h AEL onwards.
source: Detailed observation of distal cells of salivary glands revealed that SGs enlarge from 96 h AEL onwards (Figure 1D; Ma and Brill, 2021b; Neuman et al., 2021), a phenomenon that we quantified by measuring SG diameter (Figure 1D and Table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1, supported by citations.

claim: At 96–100 h AEL nascent SGs are smaller than 1 μm in diameter.
source: At 96–100 h AEL nascent SGs are smaller than 1 μm in diameter.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Up to 112 h AEL, most SGs are smaller than 3 μm in diameter and classified as 'Immature SGs'.
source: Later, and up to 112 h AEL, most SGs are smaller than 3 μm in diameter, and classified them as 'Immature SGs'.
evidence: This is an observation and classification from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: From 112 h AEL onwards most SGs are bigger than 3 μm in diameter and classified as 'Mature SGs'.
source: From 112 h AEL onwards most SGs are bigger than 3 μm in diameter and classified as 'Mature SGs' (Figure 1D and Table 1).
evidence: This is an observation and classification from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: The maximal SG diameter detected was 7.13 μm at 116–120 h AEL.
source: The maximal SG diameter that we detected was 7.13 μm at 116–120 h AEL, just before exocytosis (Table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Silencing of any of the eight subunits of the exocyst complex results in retention of Sgs3-GFP in salivary glands of prepupae.
source: Using this approach, we found that the exocyst complex is apparently required for exocytosis of SGs, since silencing of any of the eight subunits of the complex results in retention of Sgs3-GFP in salivary glands of prepupae (Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control prepupae are able to expel Sgs3 outside the puparium.
source: We analyzed Sgs3-GFP distribution in wandering larvae and prepupae (Figure 2A, B), and observed that whereas control prepupae were able to expel Sgs3 outside the puparium (Figure 2A', C), this process was blocked in most individuals expressing RNAis against any of the exocyst subunits, with Sgs3-GFP being detected inside salivary glands of prepupae (Figure 2B', C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of RNAis against any of the exocyst subunits blocks Sgs3 expulsion outside the puparium.
source: We analyzed Sgs3-GFP distribution in wandering larvae and prepupae (Figure 2A, B), and observed that whereas control prepupae were able to expel Sgs3 outside the puparium (Figure 2A', C), this process was blocked in most individuals expressing RNAis against any of the exocyst subunits, with Sgs3-GFP being detected inside salivary glands of prepupae (Figure 2B', C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All exocyst subunits are required for exocytosis of SGs.
source: These observations suggest that all exocyst subunits are required for exocytosis of SGs (Table 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing that silencing any subunit blocks exocytosis.

claim: Control salivary gland cells at 116 h AEL are filled with mature SGs.
source: Whereas control salivary gland cells were filled with mature SGs (Figure 3A), a more heterogeneous situation was found in salivary gland cells expressing RNAi against exocyst subunits, with some cells displaying mature SGs, and others, immature SGs, while even some displayed Sgs3-GFP in a mesh- or network-like structure (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Salivary gland cells expressing RNAi against exocyst subunits display a heterogeneous phenotype with some cells showing mature SGs, others immature SGs, and some showing Sgs3-GFP in a mesh-like structure.
source: Whereas control salivary gland cells were filled with mature SGs (Figure 3A), a more heterogeneous situation was found in salivary gland cells expressing RNAi against exocyst subunits, with some cells displaying mature SGs, and others, immature SGs, while even some displayed Sgs3-GFP in a mesh- or network-like structure (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of exocyst subunit RNAis at high temperatures (29°C) results in phenotypes consistent with early arrest of the secretory pathway.
source: Whereas expression of a control RNAi resulted in mature SGs irrespectively of the temperature, expression of exocyst subunits RNAis at high temperatures (29°C) resulted, as a general rule, in phenotypes consistent with early arrest of the secretory pathway, since in most cells Sgs3-GFP was retained in a reticular structure or packed in immature SGs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3.

claim: Lowering the temperature of RNAi expression allows progression of the secretory pathway.
source: By lowering the temperature of RNAi expression, and therefore moderating silencing, the most severe phenotypes (early arrest of the secretory pathway) gradually became less prominent and simultaneously, the proportion of cells displaying immature SGs, and even mature SGs, became more noticeable (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3), suggesting that lower expression of RNAis allowed the progression of the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an observation and inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3.

claim: For each RNAi tested there is a temperature at which each of the three phenotypic outcomes can be clearly identified.
source: Notably, for each of the RNAis tested there was a temperature at which each of the three phenotypic outcomes could be clearly identified, although this particular temperature could be different for each RNAi, likely due to expression levels of the transgenes (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3.

claim: Different culturing temperatures result in different degrees of silencing of exocyst subunit mRNAs.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed that different culturing temperatures resulted in different degrees of silencing of exocyst subunit mRNAs, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for exo70 and sec3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Different phenotypic outcomes from different RNAi transgenic lines targeting the same subunit are due to differences in the levels of mRNA downregulation.
source: Also, we found that different phenotypic outcomes resulting from expression of different RNAi transgenic lines that target the same subunit (exo70) are due to differences in the levels of mRNA downregulation generated by each particular RNAi (exo70 RNAiV or exo70RNAiBL), and that there is a correlation between the level of mRNA downregulation and the strength of the phenotype observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Irrespectively of the temperature of expression of RNAis, retention of SGs in salivary gland cells was always significantly higher in exocyst knock-down individuals as compared to controls.
source: Importantly, irrespectively of the temperature of expression of RNAis, retention of SGs in salivary gland cells was always significantly higher in exocyst knock-down individuals as compared to controls (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ultimately, the exocyst is required for SG exocytosis.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The exocyst is required for SG exocytosis.
source: Importantly, irrespectively of the temperature of expression of RNAis, retention of SGs in salivary gland cells was always significantly higher in exocyst knock-down individuals as compared to controls (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ultimately, the exocyst is required for SG exocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing that exocyst knock-down blocks SG exocytosis.

claim: The early-most manifestation of the requirement of the exocyst in the secretory pathway is the reticular or mesh-like phenotype obtained by strong silencing (29°C) of any of the subunits.
source: The early-most manifestation of the requirement of the exocyst in the secretory pathway was the reticular or mesh-like phenotype obtained by strong silencing (29°C) of any of the subunits (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mesh-like phenotype is reminiscent of mutants in which Sgs3 is retained at ER exit sites or at ER–Golgi complex (GC) contact sites.
source: This phenotype was reminiscent of mutants in which Sgs3 is retained at ER exit sites or at ER–Golgi complex (GC) contact sites (Burgess et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2019), suggesting that knock-down of the exocyst may provoke Sgs3 retention at the ER or GC, blocking SG biogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to previously published mutants, supported by citations.

claim: Knock-down of the exocyst may provoke Sgs3 retention at the ER or GC, blocking SG biogenesis.
source: This phenotype was reminiscent of mutants in which Sgs3 is retained at ER exit sites or at ER–Golgi complex (GC) contact sites (Burgess et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2019), suggesting that knock-down of the exocyst may provoke Sgs3 retention at the ER or GC, blocking SG biogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed phenotype and comparison to previous work.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of sec15, sec3 or sec10 provokes Sgs3 retention in the ER.
source: Indeed, we found that RNAi-mediated silencing of sec15,sec3 or sec10 provoked Sgs3 retention in the ER, since it colocalized with ER markers, as indicated by Pearson's coefficient, whereas in control larvae Sgs3-GFP was inside SGs, at a comparable developmental stage (Figure 4B–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In control larvae Sgs3-GFP is inside SGs at a comparable developmental stage.
source: Indeed, we found that RNAi-mediated silencing of sec15,sec3 or sec10 provoked Sgs3 retention in the ER, since it colocalized with ER markers, as indicated by Pearson's coefficient, whereas in control larvae Sgs3-GFP was inside SGs, at a comparable developmental stage (Figure 4B–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP-Sec15 associates closely with the trans-Golgi marker RFP-Golgi in salivary glands just prior to SG biogenesis.
source: We analyzed in detail GFP-Sec15 subcellular localization, and found that it associated closely with the trans-Golgi marker RFP-Golgi, but not with the ER marker KDEL-RFP in salivary glands just prior to SG biogenesis (Figure 5 and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 1–3.

claim: GFP-Sec15 does not associate with the ER marker KDEL-RFP in salivary glands just prior to SG biogenesis.
source: We analyzed in detail GFP-Sec15 subcellular localization, and found that it associated closely with the trans-Golgi marker RFP-Golgi, but not with the ER marker KDEL-RFP in salivary glands just prior to SG biogenesis (Figure 5 and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 1–3.

claim: The association between GFP-Sec15 and the trans-Golgi is lost after the onset of SG biogenesis.
source: This association was lost after the onset SG biogenesis, suggesting that the exocyst associates with the GC at the specific developmental stage when Sgs3 transits through that organelle (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: The exocyst associates with the GC at the specific developmental stage when Sgs3 transits through that organelle.
source: This association was lost after the onset SG biogenesis, suggesting that the exocyst associates with the GC at the specific developmental stage when Sgs3 transits through that organelle (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Sec15 associates with the Golgi before SG biogenesis and dissociates after.

claim: Exocyst silencing under conditions that block Sgs3-GFP in the ER severely affects both cis and trans-GC structures.
source: In line with this, we found that exocyst silencing under conditions that block Sgs3-GFP in the ER (29°C), both cis and trans-CG structures were severely affected (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the stage of salivary gland development when Sgs3 transits through the Golgi, the exocyst complex localizes at the GC where it is required to maintain cis- and trans-GC morphology.
source: This suggests that at this stage of salivary gland development the exocyst complex localizes at the GC, where it is required to maintain cis- and trans-GC morphology, thereby allowing the correct transport of Sgs3 from the ER to the GC (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations that Sec15 localizes to the Golgi and that exocyst silencing disrupts Golgi morphology and blocks Sgs3 transport.

claim: The exocyst is required to maintain cis- and trans-GC morphology, thereby allowing the correct transport of Sgs3 from the ER to the GC.
source: This suggests that at this stage of salivary gland development the exocyst complex localizes at the GC, where it is required to maintain cis- and trans-GC morphology, thereby allowing the correct transport of Sgs3 from the ER to the GC (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations that exocyst silencing disrupts Golgi morphology and blocks Sgs3 transport.

claim: Appropriate silencing of any of the exocyst subunits can result in accumulation of immature SGs.
source: Given that appropriate silencing conditions of any of the exocyst subunits can result in accumulation of immature SGs (Figure 7A), we set out to investigate a potential role of the exocyst in SG maturation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SG maturation involves homotypic fusion between immature SGs.
source: SG maturation is a multifaceted process that involves, among other events, homotypic fusion between immature SGs (Du et al., 2016; Neuman and Bashirullah, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GFP-Sec15 often localizes in discrete foci in between immature SGs (75% of total GFP-Sec15).
source: We found that GFP-Sec15 often localized in discrete foci in between immature SGs (75% of total GFP-Sec15), but this localization drops dramatically when SGs have undergone maturation (15%) (Figure 7B, C and Videos 4–5).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7B, C and Videos 4–5.

claim: GFP-Sec15 localization in between SGs drops dramatically when SGs have undergone maturation (15%).
source: We found that GFP-Sec15 often localized in discrete foci in between immature SGs (75% of total GFP-Sec15), but this localization drops dramatically when SGs have undergone maturation (15%) (Figure 7B, C and Videos 4–5).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7B, C and Videos 4–5.

claim: The transient localization of GFP-Sec15 supports the notion of a role of the exocyst in SG homofusion.
source: This transient localization of GFP-Sec15 supports the notion of a role of the exocyst in SG homofusion, which was confirmed by live imaging of salivary glands ex vivo (Figure 7D and Video 6).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Sec15 localizes between immature SGs and dissociates after maturation, confirmed by live imaging.

claim: Live imaging of salivary glands ex vivo confirms a role of the exocyst in SG homofusion.
source: This transient localization of GFP-Sec15 supports the notion of a role of the exocyst in SG homofusion, which was confirmed by live imaging of salivary glands ex vivo (Figure 7D and Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Video 6.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-Sec15 at 25°C results in unusually large SGs of up to 20 μm in diameter.
source: In support to this notion, when GFP-Sec15 was overexpressed at 25°C, unusually large SGs of up to 20 μm in diameter could be detected, a size never observed in control salivary glands overexpressing GFP alone (Figure 7E–H), indicating that overexpression of the Sec15 subunit alone is sufficient to induce homotypic fusion between SGs, which is in agreement with reports that indicate that Sec15 functions as a seed for exocyst complex assembly (Escrevente et al., 2021; Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7E–H.

claim: Unusually large SGs (up to 20 μm) are never observed in control salivary glands overexpressing GFP alone.
source: In support to this notion, when GFP-Sec15 was overexpressed at 25°C, unusually large SGs of up to 20 μm in diameter could be detected, a size never observed in control salivary glands overexpressing GFP alone (Figure 7E–H), indicating that overexpression of the Sec15 subunit alone is sufficient to induce homotypic fusion between SGs, which is in agreement with reports that indicate that Sec15 functions as a seed for exocyst complex assembly (Escrevente et al., 2021; Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7E–H.

claim: Overexpression of the Sec15 subunit alone is sufficient to induce homotypic fusion between SGs.
source: In support to this notion, when GFP-Sec15 was overexpressed at 25°C, unusually large SGs of up to 20 μm in diameter could be detected, a size never observed in control salivary glands overexpressing GFP alone (Figure 7E–H), indicating that overexpression of the Sec15 subunit alone is sufficient to induce homotypic fusion between SGs, which is in agreement with reports that indicate that Sec15 functions as a seed for exocyst complex assembly (Escrevente et al., 2021; Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Sec15 overexpression leads to oversized SGs, supported by citations indicating Sec15's role in exocyst assembly.

claim: Sec15 functions as a seed for exocyst complex assembly.
source: In support to this notion, when GFP-Sec15 was overexpressed at 25°C, unusually large SGs of up to 20 μm in diameter could be detected, a size never observed in control salivary glands overexpressing GFP alone (Figure 7E–H), indicating that overexpression of the Sec15 subunit alone is sufficient to induce homotypic fusion between SGs, which is in agreement with reports that indicate that Sec15 functions as a seed for exocyst complex assembly (Escrevente et al., 2021; Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of Sec8 does not have an effect on homotypic fusion of SGs.
source: In contrast, overexpression of Sec8, which is not expected to induce the formation of the whole complex, did not have an effect on homotypic fusion of SGs (Figure 7F, H).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7F, H.

claim: The characteristic localization of GFP-Sec15 foci in between adjacent immature SGs supports the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
source: The characteristic localization of GFP-Sec15 foci in between adjacent immature SGs, the fact that Sec15 overexpression results in oversized SGs, and the observation that downregulation of any subunit of the exocyst complex at appropriate levels results in accumulation of immature SGs, weigh in favor of the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple observations: Sec15 localization, Sec15 overexpression effects, and exocyst downregulation effects.

claim: Sec15 overexpression results in oversized SGs, supporting the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
source: The characteristic localization of GFP-Sec15 foci in between adjacent immature SGs, the fact that Sec15 overexpression results in oversized SGs, and the observation that downregulation of any subunit of the exocyst complex at appropriate levels results in accumulation of immature SGs, weigh in favor of the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple observations: Sec15 localization, Sec15 overexpression effects, and exocyst downregulation effects.

claim: Downregulation of any subunit of the exocyst complex at appropriate levels results in accumulation of immature SGs, supporting the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
source: The characteristic localization of GFP-Sec15 foci in between adjacent immature SGs, the fact that Sec15 overexpression results in oversized SGs, and the observation that downregulation of any subunit of the exocyst complex at appropriate levels results in accumulation of immature SGs, weigh in favor of the notion that the exocyst plays a critical role in SG homotypic fusion.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple observations: Sec15 localization, Sec15 overexpression effects, and exocyst downregulation effects.

claim: Maturation of SGs involves the incorporation of specific proteins required for homotypic fusion, apical navigation, or fusion with the apical plasma membrane.
source: Besides homotypic fusion, maturation of SGs involves the incorporation of specific proteins that are required for homotypic fusion, apical navigation, or fusion with the apical plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SG maturation.

claim: The mechanisms by which maturation factors associate with SGs are not well understood.
source: The mechanisms by which these maturation factors associate with SGs are not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt-1) is a calcium sensor.
source: One of such proteins is the calcium sensor Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt-1), which localized at the basolateral membrane of salivary gland cells before SG biogenesis (96 h AEL) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), and later became detectable on the membrane of nascent SGs (diameter <1 μm), prior to homotypic fusion (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Syt-1.

claim: Syt-1 localizes at the basolateral membrane of salivary gland cells before SG biogenesis (96 h AEL).
source: One of such proteins is the calcium sensor Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt-1), which localized at the basolateral membrane of salivary gland cells before SG biogenesis (96 h AEL) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), and later became detectable on the membrane of nascent SGs (diameter <1 μm), prior to homotypic fusion (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Syt-1 becomes detectable on the membrane of nascent SGs (diameter <1 μm), prior to homotypic fusion.
source: One of such proteins is the calcium sensor Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt-1), which localized at the basolateral membrane of salivary gland cells before SG biogenesis (96 h AEL) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), and later became detectable on the membrane of nascent SGs (diameter <1 μm), prior to homotypic fusion (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: As SGs mature, the presence of Syt-1 on SGs becomes more prominent, with a sharp increase after SG homofusion.
source: As SGs mature, the presence of Syt-1 on SGs became more prominent, with a sharp increase after SG homofusion (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D), suggesting that recruitment of Syt-1 to SGs continued after homotypic fusion had occurred (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Recruitment of Syt-1 to SGs continues after homotypic fusion has occurred.
source: As SGs mature, the presence of Syt-1 on SGs became more prominent, with a sharp increase after SG homofusion (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D), suggesting that recruitment of Syt-1 to SGs continued after homotypic fusion had occurred (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Syt-1 levels increase sharply after homofusion.

claim: Downregulation of Sec5 or Sec3 to levels that generate immature SGs significantly reduces the presence of Syt-1 on their membranes.
source: Downregulation of the exocyst subunits Sec5 or Sec3 to levels that generate immature SGs significantly reduced the presence of Syt-1 on their membranes, as compared to immature SGs of control salivary glands (Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Weaker knock-down of exocyst subunits, which allows the formation of mature SGs, improves but does not completely restore Syt-1 recruitment.
source: Interestingly, weaker knock-down, which allowed the formation of mature SGs, improved but not completely restored Syt-1 recruitment, compared to control salivary cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–F), indicating that Syt-1 is recruited to mature SGs in an exocyst-dependent manner (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Syt-1 is recruited to mature SGs in an exocyst-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, weaker knock-down, which allowed the formation of mature SGs, improved but not completely restored Syt-1 recruitment, compared to control salivary cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–F), indicating that Syt-1 is recruited to mature SGs in an exocyst-dependent manner (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exocyst knock-down reduces Syt-1 recruitment.

claim: CD63 is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian Tsp29Fa.
source: CD63, the Drosophila homolog of mammalian Tsp29Fa, is another protein required for SG maturation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD63.

claim: CD63 is required for SG maturation.
source: CD63, the Drosophila homolog of mammalian Tsp29Fa, is another protein required for SG maturation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD63.

claim: CD63 localizes at the apical plasma membrane before SG formation.
source: CD63 localizes at the apical plasma membrane before SG formation, and reaches the membrane of SGs through endosomal retrograde trafficking (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, supported by citation.

claim: CD63 reaches the membrane of SGs through endosomal retrograde trafficking.
source: CD63 localizes at the apical plasma membrane before SG formation, and reaches the membrane of SGs through endosomal retrograde trafficking (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD63 can be readily detected at the membrane of 1, 3, or 5 μm SGs.
source: We investigated if the exocyst participates in recruitment of CD63 to SGs, and found that CD63 could be readily detected at the membrane of 1, 3, or 5 μm SGs (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–H), while upon Sec5 or Sec3 downregulation CD63 was significantly reduced on immature SGs (Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: Upon Sec5 or Sec3 downregulation CD63 is significantly reduced on immature SGs.
source: We investigated if the exocyst participates in recruitment of CD63 to SGs, and found that CD63 could be readily detected at the membrane of 1, 3, or 5 μm SGs (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–H), while upon Sec5 or Sec3 downregulation CD63 was significantly reduced on immature SGs (Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: Milder reduction of Sec3 expression, under conditions that allow the formation of mature SGs, does not affect CD63 recruitment to SGs.
source: Interestingly, milder reduction of Sec3 expression, under conditions that allow the formation of mature SGs, did not affect CD63 recruitment to SGs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2J–L), indicating that CD63 is recruited to SGs before homotypic fusion in an exocyst-dependent manner and that, unlike to Syt-1, recruitment ceases after homotypic fusion has occurred (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2J–L.

claim: CD63 is recruited to SGs before homotypic fusion in an exocyst-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, milder reduction of Sec3 expression, under conditions that allow the formation of mature SGs, did not affect CD63 recruitment to SGs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2J–L), indicating that CD63 is recruited to SGs before homotypic fusion in an exocyst-dependent manner and that, unlike to Syt-1, recruitment ceases after homotypic fusion has occurred (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exocyst knock-down reduces CD63 on immature SGs but not on mature SGs.

claim: Unlike Syt-1, CD63 recruitment ceases after homotypic fusion has occurred.
source: Interestingly, milder reduction of Sec3 expression, under conditions that allow the formation of mature SGs, did not affect CD63 recruitment to SGs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2J–L), indicating that CD63 is recruited to SGs before homotypic fusion in an exocyst-dependent manner and that, unlike to Syt-1, recruitment ceases after homotypic fusion has occurred (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that CD63 levels do not increase after homofusion, unlike Syt-1.

claim: Rab11 and Rab1 are required for SG maturation.
source: The small GTPases Rab11 and Rab1 were reported to be required for SG maturation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab11 and Rab1.

claim: Rab11 associates to SGs independently of their size.
source: Whereas Rab11 associates to SGs independently of their size, Rab1 was found transiently on immature SGs only (Ma and Brill, 2021a; Neuman et al., 2021), and moreover, Rab1 recruitment to SGs depends on Rab11 (Neuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rab1 is found transiently on immature SGs only.
source: Whereas Rab11 associates to SGs independently of their size, Rab1 was found transiently on immature SGs only (Ma and Brill, 2021a; Neuman et al., 2021), and moreover, Rab1 recruitment to SGs depends on Rab11 (Neuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rab1 recruitment to SGs depends on Rab11.
source: Whereas Rab11 associates to SGs independently of their size, Rab1 was found transiently on immature SGs only (Ma and Brill, 2021a; Neuman et al., 2021), and moreover, Rab1 recruitment to SGs depends on Rab11 (Neuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Silencing of Sec5 under conditions that allow the formation of immature SGs provokes significant reduction of Rab1-YFP on the SG membrane.
source: In fact, silencing of Sec5 under conditions that allowed the formation of immature SGs provoked significant reduction of Rab1-YFP on the SG membrane (Figure 8G–I), suggesting that the exocyst participated in Rab1 recruitment (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8G–I.

claim: The exocyst participates in Rab1 recruitment to SGs.
source: In fact, silencing of Sec5 under conditions that allowed the formation of immature SGs provoked significant reduction of Rab1-YFP on the SG membrane (Figure 8G–I), suggesting that the exocyst participated in Rab1 recruitment (Figure 8M).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exocyst knock-down reduces Rab1 on SGs.

claim: Immature SGs resulting from Sec5 or Sec3 knock-down display higher-than-normal levels of YFP-Rab11 around them.
source: Remarkably, immature SGs that resulted from Sec5 or Sec3 knock-down displayed higher-than-normal levels of YFP-Rab11 around them (Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–O), suggesting that the exocyst is a negative regulator of Rab11 recruitment.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–O.

claim: The exocyst is a negative regulator of Rab11 recruitment to SGs.
source: Remarkably, immature SGs that resulted from Sec5 or Sec3 knock-down displayed higher-than-normal levels of YFP-Rab11 around them (Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–O), suggesting that the exocyst is a negative regulator of Rab11 recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exocyst knock-down increases Rab11 on SGs.

claim: Overexpression of a constitutively active form of Rab11 (UAS-YFP-Rab11CA) provokes an arrest of SG maturation.
source: Noteworthy, overexpression of a constitutively active form of Rab11 (UAS-YFP-Rab11CA), which was readily recruited to SGs, also provoked an arrest of SG maturation, thereby phenocopying exocyst complex knock-down (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active Rab11 phenocopies exocyst complex knock-down.
source: Noteworthy, overexpression of a constitutively active form of Rab11 (UAS-YFP-Rab11CA), which was readily recruited to SGs, also provoked an arrest of SG maturation, thereby phenocopying exocyst complex knock-down (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: During maturation of SGs, the levels of active Rab11 need to be precisely regulated.
source: Thus, during maturation of SGs, the levels of active Rab11 need to be precisely regulated, and this is achieved, at least in part, by the exocyst (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations that both exocyst knock-down (which increases Rab11) and Rab11 overexpression block SG maturation.

claim: Precise regulation of active Rab11 levels during SG maturation is achieved, at least in part, by the exocyst.
source: Thus, during maturation of SGs, the levels of active Rab11 need to be precisely regulated, and this is achieved, at least in part, by the exocyst (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations that the exocyst negatively regulates Rab11 recruitment.

claim: The exocyst is an effector of different Rab-GTPases during vesicle exocytosis.
source: Given that the exocyst is an effector of different Rab-GTPases during vesicle exocytosis (Guo et al., 1999; Novick et al., 1995; Wu et al., 2005), we next investigated if Rab11 is required for recruiting the exocyst to SGs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sec15 fails to localize on SGs following knock-down of Rab11.
source: Indeed, we found that Sec15 failed to localize on SGs following knock-down of Rab11 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating a crucial role of Rab11 in recruitment of Sec15, and probably of the whole exocyst to SGs.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E.

claim: Rab11 plays a crucial role in recruitment of Sec15 to SGs.
source: Indeed, we found that Sec15 failed to localize on SGs following knock-down of Rab11 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating a crucial role of Rab11 in recruitment of Sec15, and probably of the whole exocyst to SGs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Rab11 knock-down prevents Sec15 localization to SGs.

claim: Rab11 probably recruits the whole exocyst to SGs.
source: Indeed, we found that Sec15 failed to localize on SGs following knock-down of Rab11 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating a crucial role of Rab11 in recruitment of Sec15, and probably of the whole exocyst to SGs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Rab11 recruits Sec15 and the knowledge that Sec15 is part of the exocyst complex.

claim: Rab11 recruits Sec15, and perhaps the whole exocyst, to immature SGs to allow homotypic fusion and maturation.
source: Overall, the results described in this section suggest that Rab11 recruits Sec15, and perhaps the whole exocyst, to immature SGs to allow homotypic fusion and maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), while in turn, the exocyts limits the levels and/or activity of Rab11 on SGs (Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–R), as excessive Rab11 is apparently detrimental for SG maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations that Rab11 recruits Sec15 and that the exocyst is required for SG maturation.

claim: The exocyst limits the levels and/or activity of Rab11 on SGs.
source: Overall, the results described in this section suggest that Rab11 recruits Sec15, and perhaps the whole exocyst, to immature SGs to allow homotypic fusion and maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), while in turn, the exocyts limits the levels and/or activity of Rab11 on SGs (Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–R), as excessive Rab11 is apparently detrimental for SG maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exocyst knock-down increases Rab11 on SGs.

claim: Excessive Rab11 is detrimental for SG maturation.
source: Overall, the results described in this section suggest that Rab11 recruits Sec15, and perhaps the whole exocyst, to immature SGs to allow homotypic fusion and maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D, E), while in turn, the exocyts limits the levels and/or activity of Rab11 on SGs (Figure 8J–L and Figure 8—figure supplement 2M–R), as excessive Rab11 is apparently detrimental for SG maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Rab11 overexpression blocks SG maturation.

claim: A single-negative feedback loop precisely regulates Rab11 and exocyst complex activity/levels, controlling recruitment of maturation factors such as Syt-1, CD63, and Rab1.
source: We propose that a single-negative feedback loop precisely regulates Rab11 and exocyst complex activity/levels, thus controlling recruitment of maturation factors such as Syt-1, CD63, and Rab1, and therefore, the outcome of SG maturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Under low silencing conditions of exocyst subunits the prevalent phenotype is mature SGs retained in salivary gland cells.
source: Under low silencing conditions of exocyst subunits the prevalent phenotype was mature SGs retained in salivary gland cells (Figures 3D and 9A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a function of the complex in SG fusion with the apical plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 9A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The exocyst complex has a function in SG fusion with the apical plasma membrane.
source: Under low silencing conditions of exocyst subunits the prevalent phenotype was mature SGs retained in salivary gland cells (Figures 3D and 9A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a function of the complex in SG fusion with the apical plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that low exocyst silencing leads to retention of mature SGs.

claim: The process of SG–plasma membrane fusion can be assessed by visualizing the incorporation of plasma membrane-specific components to the membrane of SGs.
source: The process of SG–plasma membrane fusion can be assessed by visualizing the incorporation of plasma membrane-specific components to the membrane of SGs (de la Riva-Carrasco et al., 2021; Rousso et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established methodology supported by citations.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) is a lipid of the inner leaflet of the apical plasma membrane.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) is a lipid of the inner leaflet of the apical plasma membrane, which is absent in endomembranes (Phan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is absent in endomembranes.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) is a lipid of the inner leaflet of the apical plasma membrane, which is absent in endomembranes (Phan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Using a fluorophore-based reporter of PI(4,5)P2, SGs that have fused with the plasma membrane can be distinguished from those that have not.
source: Using a fluorophore-based reporter of PI(4,5)P2 the SGs that have fused with the plasma membrane can be distinguished from those that have not.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the properties of PI(4,5)P2.

claim: Silencing of Exo70 impairs fusion of SGs with the plasma membrane.
source: Using this approach, we found that silencing of Exo70 impaired fusion with the plasma membrane (Figure 9B–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 9B–D.

claim: At the stage of SG exocytosis, GFP-Sec15 is no longer detected between SGs, but rather at sites of contact of SGs with the plasma membrane.
